newsitem.title: CHINA: China hails market and end of central planning.
newsitem.headline: China hails market and end of central planning.

text.p: China on Thursday hailed the wisdom of its decision to scrap its communist planned economy, saying management by edict had failed to eliminate scarcity and only the market could make the nation rich and strong.

"The words 'Market Economy' have been writ large on the flag of socialism for the first time," crowed the People's Daily in a front-page editorial issued in the run-up to a crucial Communist Party congress in September or October.
The editorial was the party mouthpiece's latest warning to die-hard leftist members trying to rekindle a debate on the merits of socialism and capitalism.

Nearly two decades of reform had shown that building a "socialist market economy" -- Beijing's catch-phrase for the combination of capitalist methods and communist rhetoric -- was the only way to prosperity, the People's Daily said.

"Only socialism can save China and only the socialist market economy can develop China. This is the conclusion of history," the newspaper said in a spirited defence of market economics and price competition.

"We ran a planned economy for more than 20 years and created the foundations of industrialisation, but it was still an economy of scarcity and an economy of poverty," it said. It added that urban and rural incomes had grown little under central control.
In the years since the launch of economic reform in the late 1970s, by contrast, urban residents had seen their incomes surge and farmers had found the road to basic prosperity, it said.

Capitalist-style reforms launched by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping have come under increasing fire from China's ultra-leftists in recent months, prompting leaders to order a spate of state press commentaries aimed at squashing such criticism before the 15th party congress.

Critics of fast-track reform of the lumbering state sector have often focused on rampant corruption, the loss of state assets and the threat of instability -- but the People's Daily said such issues showed reform should be faster, not slower.

"The challenge comes from our unfamiliarity with the market economy and from our lack of knowledge of market economy methods," it said, dismissing suggestions that disorder and graft were inevitable companions of a market system.

Party reformers and hardliners have been jostling for position in the run-up to the five-yearly congress, which will set the path of the world's most populous nation and select leaders who will take China into the 21st century.
Much of the political groundwork for the congress is being done behind closed doors at an annual summer gathering of party leaders at the beachside resort of Beidaihe.

President Jiang Zemin has thrown his weight behind efforts to shake up the state-run sector, which has been unable to compete with nimbler rivals in the private sector, and has been edging closer to shutting down or selling off hopeless state firms.

More courage was needed in pursuing market reforms, said the People's Daily. Its commentary was run alongside columns of praise for China's system of "stock cooperation" under which workers take a stake in formerly state-owned firms.
Such unique approaches were needed to assure the success of China's economic reform, a project that was unprecedented but for which there was no alternative, the newspaper said.
"Ahead is a new world, there is no way back," it said.
